title: Nesting and Counting
focus: Recursive structure in flat input, ordered traversal with an early exit, and the DP that counts rather than optimises.

cards.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
patterns: Track start and length, not the string
cards.trigger: Find the longest symmetric run inside a string.
cards.recall: Write it from memory, both centre types. Then answer: why track `(start, length)` instead of slicing the substring each time you improve?
useWhen: Longest palindromic substring
Count palindromic substrings
Palindrome partitioning, with a precomputed table
Shortest palindrome by prefix reversal
Any question about maximal symmetric runs
template: while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:
return l + 1, r - 1        # step back inside the last valid window
for l, r in (expand(i, i), expand(i, i + 1)):   # odd then even
return s[start:end + 1]        # slice ONCE, at the end
keyInsights: The `l + 1, r - 1` return is where off-by-one errors live. The loop exits one step past the valid window
Slicing inside the loop makes it O(n^3) on adversarial input. Carry indices and slice once
Every index needs two expansions, odd-centred and even-centred. Forgetting the even case fails on 'abba'
cards.trap: 'Longest palindromic SUBSEQUENCE.' Completely different problem: interval DP, dp[i][j], O(n^2) time and space. Do not let the similar name pull you into the wrong solution.

cards.title: Nested Decoding with a Stack
cards.trigger: Flat input with recursive structure: brackets, nesting, or a grammar you must evaluate.
cards.recall: Write the decode-string solver from memory. Then answer: exactly what gets pushed when you hit an opening bracket, and why is pushing only the number not enough?
useWhen: Decode nested repeat strings
Basic calculator with parentheses and unary minus
Flatten a nested list or nested iterator
Evaluate a nested boolean or arithmetic expression
Simplify a Unix path, a degenerate case of the same idea
template: stack.append((cur, num))      # park the OUTER context
cur, num = '', 0              # start a fresh inner context
cur = prev + cur * k          # fold the inner result into the outer
# Calculator shape: push (result_so_far, sign) on '(' and fold on ')'
# Path simplify: split on '/', push a name, pop on '..', ignore '.' and ''
keyInsights: You must push both the accumulated outer string and the count. Pushing only the count loses everything before the bracket
`num = num * 10 + int(ch)` is how you handle counts above nine. Single-digit assumptions fail the hidden tests
Every one of these is 'recursion done with an explicit stack'. If the recursive version is clearer, write that instead and say why
cards.trap: 'Now support nested negative numbers and spaces.' The tokeniser becomes the hard part, not the stack. Separate tokenising from evaluating before you write a line.

cards.title: Ordered Traversal with Early Exit
cards.trigger: You need the kth element in sorted order from a BST, and k is much smaller than n.
cards.recall: Write the iterative inorder from memory, including the exact push-left-then-pop structure. Then answer the design follow-up: if kth-smallest is called constantly and the tree is modified, what do you change?
useWhen: Kth smallest or kth largest in a BST
Validate a BST by checking inorder is increasing
Convert a BST to a sorted list or a doubly linked list
Find the inorder successor of a node
Range sum in a BST, prune branches outside the range
template: while node:                # go as far left as possible
node = node.right          # then the right subtree
# Kth LARGEST: same loop, mirrored (right first, then left)
# If queries are frequent AND the tree mutates: store subtree size per node.
# Then kth becomes an O(h) descent:
#   otherwise               -> go right with k -= left_size + 1

problem.name: Kth Smallest Element in a BST

keyInsights: O(h + k), not O(n). Saying the tighter bound shows you understand that the early exit is the point
The size-augmented version is the expected answer to the frequent-queries follow-up, and it is O(h) per query
The inner while-push-left plus outer pop is the canonical iterative inorder. Learn it once, use it everywhere
cards.trap: 'Do it recursively with O(1) space.' Morris traversal threads the tree temporarily. Name it, say it mutates during traversal, and offer the stack version as the safe one.

cards.title: Counting DP with Validity
cards.trigger: Count the ways to parse or tile a sequence, where each step has one or two valid moves.
cards.recall: Write decode ways from memory. Then answer the case that breaks everyone: what happens at a '0', and what happens at '06'?
useWhen: Decode a digit string into letters
Count tilings of a 1 by n board with pieces of size 1 and 2
Count valid parse trees or expression groupings
Staircase problems with forbidden steps
Any Fibonacci-shaped count with a per-step legality check
template: # dp[i] = number of ways to decode s[:i]
if not s or s[0] == '0': return 0
if cur == 0: return 0                 # dead end, e.g. '30'
keyInsights: '0' can never stand alone, and can only be consumed as part of 10 or 20. Every failing test is a zero
The leading `10 <=` matters: '06' is not 6, it is invalid. String-to-int silently hides that unless you range check
dp[0] = 1 means 'one way to decode nothing'. That is the base case that makes the two-digit branch work at i = 1
cards.trap: 'Now the string can contain a wildcard star matching 1 through 9.' The branch count explodes into cases and you need modular arithmetic. Structure the cases before coding.

cards.title: Eulerian Path
cards.trigger: Traverse every edge exactly once, typically phrased as an itinerary or a sequence reconstruction.
cards.recall: Write Hierholzer from memory. Then answer the part that makes it non-obvious: why is the route appended AFTER the recursion and then reversed?
useWhen: Reconstruct an itinerary from a set of tickets
Cracking the safe, de Bruijn sequences
Valid arrangement of pairs, domino chains
Any 'use every edge once' phrasing
Genome assembly style sequence stitching
template: heapq.heappush(adj[a], b)          # smallest lexical option first
visit(heapq.heappop(adj[u]))   # consume the edge as you take it
route.append(u)                    # append AFTER, on the way out
#   Euler CIRCUIT: every vertex has in-degree == out-degree, and is connected
#   Euler PATH:    exactly one vertex with out - in == 1 (the start),
#                  exactly one with in - out == 1 (the end)
keyInsights: Post-order append means a dead end lands at the front of the reversed route, which is exactly where it belongs
A naive greedy walk gets stuck in a dead end and cannot backtrack correctly. Hierholzer is the fix, not an optimisation
Deleting the edge as you take it is what makes 'exactly once' hold. Marking visited nodes would be wrong, edges are the resource
cards.trap: 'Is this different from a Hamiltonian path?' Yes, and enormously: every edge once is polynomial, every vertex once is NP-complete. Know that contrast cold.
